CA02.why: Same tolerance-to-absolute-value-inequality setup (machine-cut part, |L − c| ≤ tol). Here it adds a trim-and-divide step; the core is unchanged. CLD-ACT-M-000220 is the same.

CA04.why: Constant-rate projection to a target level (phone usage). Here the rate comes from two readings and the answer is a clock time.
Constant drain rate found from a reading, then the time to reach a lower level is asked.

CA05.why: Greatest value of one variable allowed by two linear inequalities, found by substituting the boundary of one into the other. This is the same as SAT-271/batch-032 Q032-03/gen01 G01 (greatest x with y ≥ 2x − 3 and y ≤ −x + 9), put in a farm context.
Same context wording ('at most N hours combined', 'at least twice as many'). SAT-069 only writes the system. CLD-SAT-M-000275 (extreme count under two constraints) is also close.

CA12.why: Two travelers on a line; asks when their separation equals a given distance. Here they approach and pass each other, and the second time is asked (gen02 H08/batch-037 Q037-02 are the same live item).

CA13.why: Fixed cost plus per-unit cost, revenue from price × units, solve for a threshold number of units (gen07 BA12 is the same). Here two break-even points are differenced.

CB02.why: Inverse variation applied to a new input (acknowledged). The inverse-square law changes the factor but the template is the same. The format also mirrors common official SAT inverse-square items.

CB03.why: Counting integers that satisfy a factorable quadratic inequality with strict endpoints. The context build (revenue − cost) is the only addition. CLD-SAT-M-000205 (interval where a quadratic is positive) is also close.

CB04.why: Same open box made by cutting corners from cardboard. Here the domain is asked, not the volume.

CB05.why: Same specific function reused: $24,000 car losing 15% per year (V = 24,000(0.85)^t). ACT-113 asks the value after 3 years (14,739); CB05's distractor D, 9,261, is 24,000 − 14,739.
RETIRED as a duplicate of ACT-113: 'A car worth $24,000 loses 15% each year; value after 2 years?' (17,340). That answer is exactly CB05's intermediate step. Change the numbers at minimum.

CB06.why: Find an unknown constant in a quadratic height model from one condition, then report the maximum height (fountain: vertex location gives b). Here the landing time gives k.

CB10.why: Upstream/downstream with d/(s − c) and d/(s + c) (acknowledged). Here it is symbolic and the round-trip time is asked.

CB11.why: Quadratic whose vertex is hidden in a condition, plus a second condition, then evaluate f at another point. SAT-381 hides the axis in f(x) = f(6 − x) with min −4 and also answers 12. CLD-SAT-M-000101 and CLD-ACT-M-000700 (vertex + one point → a) are also close.

CC02.why: Weighted-mean balance with two group values and a combined mean, solving for group size (ACT-615: juniors 72, seniors 81, overall 78). CC02 asks the same thing as a fraction (percent) instead of a count. CLD-ACT-M-000275 is the same.

CC04.why: Ratio before and after adding to the quantities, solved for a count. ACT-513 was RETIRED as a template of ACT-058: 3:5, add 6 red, becomes 3:4. Here both parts change.

CC05.why: Scale a sample proportion up to a population estimate. Here the base is area and needs a hectare conversion.

CC07.why: Percent change of a combined quantity when two factors change by percents (multiply the multipliers). SAT-294 multiplies; CC07 divides. CLD-ACT-M-000266 (unit-price percent change when the denominator changes) is also close.

CD02.why: V09 asks for A = C²/(4π) (area from circumference). CD02 hinges on V = C²h/(4π), the same substitution. Used together, one cues the other. CLD-SAT-M-000395 (cylinder from its lateral rectangle) is also close.

CD03.why: Circle tangent to two perpendicular lines puts the center at (r, r) (ACT-591 retired as its duplicate). Here the corner-to-circle gap is asked.

CD04.why: Reverse of ACT-634. ACT-634 gives two angles of elevation (30°, 60°) and the horizontal distance between them, and asks the height. CD04 gives the height and two angles (45°, 30°), and asks the difference of the horizontal distances.

CD06.why: Rise in level in a cylinder = added volume / πr². Here it is a rate with an m→cm conversion.

CD07.why: Core step is the isosceles-trapezoid area from bases and legs (height from √(leg² − half-difference²)). ACT-584 was RETIRED as a duplicate of ACT-104. Here a prism volume and a conversion to liters are added.

answer_errors.issue: The stated trap error is wrong. '1 cm³ = 10 mm³' gives 5,400 mm³ → 450 s = 0.125 h, not 1.25. The value 1.25 comes from 1 cm³ = 100 mm³ (squaring instead of cubing). The key 12.5 is correct.

Distractor B (0.32) does not follow from its stated error. Converting 15 m to 150 cm with the tree in cm gives 600 × 8/150 = 32. Getting 0.32 needs the tree left as 6 (m) with distance 150, i.e., 6 × 8/150. Fix the rationale or the value (32 would also be a mixed-unit trap). The key 3.2 is correct.

Minor: distractor A's rule (shadow = 6 tan θ) gives a shadow that gets SHORTER (6 → 3.46), so 2.5 answers 'how much shorter', not 'longer'. The value checks out but the rationale should say so. The key 4.39 → 4.4 is correct.

cues_or_overdetermined.issue: Key 64 is the largest choice, and every distractor (36, 48, 60) is an attainable value of xy + 4x. For a 'greatest possible value' item, picking the largest choice is always right. Replace a distractor with an unattainable larger value (e.g., 72 = 6·12, from a different misstep).
Same flaw: 'least possible profit' key 25 is the smallest choice, and 55, 60, 90 are all attainable profits. Choosing the minimum wins. Add a too-small distractor (e.g., 10 from 3.00 − 2.80, or 0).

Real-world plausibility cue. The key $0.58 per mile is the only realistic per-mile cost and the only choice under $1. $2.68, $20.18 and $29.00 per mile are implausible, and 29.00 is really a per-hour figure.
A quick direction check removes two choices. Moving closer must raise the reading, so 202.5 and 270 (both < 360) are out, leaving 480 vs 640.
Distractor D, 2d/(s² − c²), fails a units check (hours²/mile). Setting c = 0 leaves A, B, C all equal to 2d/s, so the remaining discrimination rests on the C sign trap only. Mild.
Mild: the mean $32 is closer to $20, so fewer than half gave $50. That eliminates 60% and 64% at once, leaving 24% vs 40%.
Mild: area grew more than birds, so density fell. That eliminates D (the increase) instantly.

likely_easier_than_labeled.why: One subtraction and division by 5. The fencepost step is a single, familiar idea.
Pair low sell with high cost. The key is also the smallest choice.
The direction check leaves two choices.
Two multiplications by 0.85 then 15%. The model is familiar.
Substitute and find the vertex. The key is also the largest choice.
Subtract, divide, square, or plug in t = 16.
One proportion with a stated conversion.
